Paving and patio cleaning in Melbourne

Paving cleaning, and the joints put back

Patios, alfresco areas, courtyards, pool surrounds and paved paths across Melbourne. Cleaning paving is half the job. The other half is replacing the jointing sand that comes out with the dirt, because empty joints are what let the weeds back and leave pavers rocking underfoot.

  • Joints re-sanded as part of the job
  • Pre-treated for moss between the pavers
  • Sealing locks the sand in
Get A Quote 0400 638 010
  1. Home
  2. Services

Why paving is different

A paved surface is not one surface. It is a few hundred small ones with a joint between each pair, and the joint is where everything happens: the moss, the weeds, the ants, the silt, and the sand that is supposed to be holding it all steady.

Cleaning a patio washes most of that sand out along with the dirt. That is not a mistake, it is unavoidable, and it is why a patio that was cleaned and left rocks underfoot and sprouts weeds within a season. Putting fresh kiln dried sand back into the joints afterwards is not an extra. It is the second half of the job and it is part of what we quote.

The life of a joint

Why your patio is moving

Most problems people describe as a paving problem are a joint problem.

STEP 01

Laid and full

Kiln dried sand swept into every joint and compacted. The pavers interlock, nothing moves and there is nowhere for a seed to land.

STEP 02

Washing out

Rain, hosing and foot traffic pull sand out of the top of the joint over a few years. The gaps open and the surface starts holding water.

STEP 03

Colonised

Moss takes the damp joint first, then weeds root in the silt that has replaced the sand. The green between pavers is almost never on the paver.

STEP 04

Moving

With the joint empty there is nothing locking the pavers to each other. They rock, the edges chip, and the levels start to go. At this point it is a relaying job rather than a cleaning one.

The job is to stop it at stage three

Cleaning and re-sanding takes a patio back to stage one. Left past stage four it becomes a landscaper's job, and that costs many times more than keeping the joints full ever would have.

By paving material

What each one takes

Paving materials behave very differently under pressure, and the joint treatment changes with them.
  How it is cleaned The joint Worth knowing
Concrete pavers Moderate pressure, pre-treated for moss Kiln dried sand Colour can be a thin face on cheaper pavers. Tested first
Clay pavers Moderate pressure, they are harder than they look Kiln dried sand Very durable. Colour is through the body so it does not fade
Bluestone Low pressure, longer dwell, test patch first Fine sand or mortar depending on the lay Porous. Stains easily and benefits most from sealing
Travertine and limestone Low pressure, neutral chemistry only Usually mortar or grout Acid damages it permanently. Never cleaned with it
Porcelain pavers Low pressure, the solution does the work Grout or open joint on pedestals Near zero porosity, so the dirt is on it rather than in it
Permeable paving Moderate, with the drainage gaps cleared Open aggregate, deliberately The gaps are the point. They are cleared, not filled

Swipe for the rest of the columns

Included in a paving clean

All of it, on every paved job.

  • Pre-treatment for moss, algae and lichen in the joints
  • Cleaning at the pressure the material takes, not the maximum available
  • Weeds and moss removed from the joints rather than just cut back
  • Silt and debris flushed out of the open joints
  • Fresh kiln dried sand swept and compacted into the joints afterwards
  • Edges, steps and the perimeter detailed by hand
  • Pots and furniture moved and replaced, beds pre-wet and rinsed

Quoted separately

Related work that is genuinely its own job.

  • Sealing, which locks the joint sand in as well as protecting the pavers. Paver sealing
  • Polymeric sand, where you want the joints set hard rather than loose
  • Relaying or re-levelling pavers that have dropped or lifted
  • Rust, oil and tannin that have soaked into the paver itself
  • Efflorescence coming out of the pavers or the bedding sand
  • Replacing cracked or chipped pavers, which we will point out
  • Repointing mortared joints where the mortar has perished

Questions

Asked about paving and patios

Will cleaning wash the sand out of my paving?

Yes, some of it, and that is unavoidable. Most of the dirt in a paved surface is in the joint, so getting the dirt out takes sand with it.

It is why re-sanding is part of the job rather than an extra. A patio cleaned and left with empty joints will rock underfoot and sprout weeds within a season, which is a worse outcome than not cleaning it.

How do I stop the weeds coming back?

Keep the joints full. Weeds do not root in a paver, they root in the silt that fills an empty joint, so a properly sanded joint gives them nothing to work with.

Two things extend that further: sealing, which binds the top of the sand so it stops washing out, and polymeric sand, which sets semi-hard in the joint. Both are quoted separately and both are worth it on a patio you use.

My pavers rock when I walk on them. Is that a cleaning problem?

Not on its own. Rocking means the pavers have lost their interlock, which is an empty joint problem first and a bedding problem second. Cleaning and re-sanding fixes it where the bedding underneath is still sound.

Where a paver has actually dropped, or the levels have gone, that is a relaying job and we will say so rather than sanding around it.

Can you clean travertine and limestone?

Yes, carefully, and never with acid. Both are calcium based, so acid dissolves the surface and leaves a permanently dull etched patch. They are cleaned at low pressure with neutral chemistry and a longer dwell.

They are also porous, so they stain more easily than concrete and they benefit more than most surfaces from being sealed afterwards.

What is the white residue on my pavers?

Usually efflorescence: salts from the paver or from the bedding sand coming to the surface with moisture. It is not dirt, and ordinary cleaning does not remove it because more keeps arriving from underneath.

It can be treated, and it recurs until the moisture path is dealt with. Efflorescence removal covers the detail.

How often should a patio be cleaned?

Every two to three years in reasonable sun, more often in a shaded courtyard where moss gets a foothold. If the joints are sealed, longer, because the sand stays put and there is far less for the moss to colonise.
